options_ranked.title: Base Oil Procurement Hedging, Supplier Renegotiation, and Cost-to-Serve Reduction
options_ranked.description: Attack the COGS side directly, which the price-lock does not constrain: renegotiate base-oil supplier terms and evaluate forward hedging instruments to stabilize feedstock cost, and run a cost-to-serve teardown on Synthetic Blend and Conventional grades to extract manufacturing yield, packaging, and distribution consolidation savings deployable within the price-lock window. First workstream is a measurement-integrity check: confirm the margin drop is a real cost shock, not an overhead-allocation artefact. Products within threshold (per the unaffected timeframe buckets) are excluded from intervention scope.
options_ranked.rationale: The intervention pulls the confirmed base_oil_cost -> COGS -> Gross Margin % chain — the only fully confirmed causal path to the root cause — and is the only option entirely untouched by the price-lock constraint because it operates on the numerator's cost side, not price.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 45–120 days (renegotiation and process levers), hedging protection accrues over subsequent quarters

arguments_for: Targets the confirmed root-cause chain (base_oil_cost sums into COGS, which directly moves Gross Margin %) rather than symptoms.
Fully compliant with the price-lock clause since no customer-facing price changes are required.
arguments_against: Supplier concessions depend on negotiating leverage; if base-oil markets are tight, renegotiation may yield little.
Hedging instruments carry premium costs and basis risk that can consume part of the projected recovery.
key_questions: What has actual base-oil landed cost done period-over-period since 2026-006, and does its magnitude reconcile to the 7.14pp decline?

arguments_for: Cost stabilization protects margin on price-locked anchor volume that no commercial lever can reach mid-quarter.
arguments_against: Ignores the revenue side entirely — leaves recoverable spot-market pricing headroom on the table.
key_questions: Should procurement savings be banked or partially reinvested in price competitiveness?

arguments_for: The audit output (is this cyclical feedstock inflation or a structural cost reset?) is the decisive input for any future portfolio participation decision.
arguments_against: If the cost shock is structural rather than cyclical, hedging only delays rather than resolves the margin problem.
key_questions: Does the base-oil cost trajectory look like a cyclical spike or a permanent step-change?

implementation_triggers: Base-oil cost decomposition confirms input inflation accounts for the majority of the COGS increase
Overhead-absorption check rules out costing-methodology artefacts
prerequisites: Decompose COGS variance since 2026-006 into base oil, manufacturing, packaging, and distribution components (all confirmed COGS categories)
Treasury sign-off on hedging instrument mandate and exposure limits
Supplier contract inventory with renewal dates and volume commitments

impact_estimate.basis: Supplier renegotiation (1.5–2.5pp), forward hedging (0.8–1.5pp), and manufacturing/packaging/distribution efficiency (0.7–1.5pp) against the 7.14pp Synthetic Blend and 6.61pp Conventional segment declines; sized to the affected engine-oil segments, not the enterprise headline.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base-oil cost inflation, not a costing/allocation artefact or discounting, is the dominant driver of the engine-oil margin decline.
key_assumptions.provenance: COGS decomposition since 2026-006 shows the Raw Materials (base oil) line accounting for the majority of the COGS increase; falsified if allocation changes or discounts explain it.

key_assumptions.assumption: COGS movements pass through directly to Gross Margin %.
key_assumptions.provenance: Confirmed client relationship: gross_margin_pct <-> cogs (direct, confirmed); base_oil_cost is a confirmed account_category component of COGS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Suppliers will concede 1.5–2.5pp-equivalent cost relief through renegotiation or term restructuring.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed supplier amendments delivering measurable per-unit base-oil cost reduction within 120 days.

options_ranked.title: Tiered Price Escalation on Synthetic Blend — Spot Repricing Plus Renewal-Cycle Pass-Through Clauses
options_ranked.description: Recover margin on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (the largest single decline, -7.14pp) through a two-tier mechanism explicitly scoped to EXCLUDE anchor accounts under the mid-quarter price-lock: (1) 3–4% ASP escalation on spot/transactional customers not bound by the price-lock clause; (2) embed base-oil cost-pass-through/indexation clauses into anchor-account contracts at their next renewal window, not mid-quarter. Compressor Oil and Hydraulic Oil follow in a second wave; segments within threshold require no intervention.
options_ranked.rationale: Pulls the confirmed net_revenue <-> gross_margin_pct relationship directly: price recovery on unconstrained volume moves the ratio without waiting for procurement outcomes. The critic finding on anchor-account exposure is answered by hard-gating the repricing list against the price-lock register before any escalation letter is issued.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 30–90 days for spot repricing; renewal-window timing for pass-through clauses

arguments_for: Directly monetizes the confirmed revenue-to-margin mechanism on the single product with the largest margin delta, without touching COGS assumptions.
Indexation clauses at renewal convert a one-time recovery into structural protection against future base-oil inflation.
arguments_against: Spot repricing risks volume leakage to competitors if the cost shock is not industry-wide.
Treats the current portfolio as fixed and does not question whether Value-category demand is worth serving at these margins.
key_questions: What share of Synthetic Blend revenue is spot/transactional vs price-locked anchor volume?
When do the next three largest anchor contracts come up for renewal?

arguments_for: Requires no capital and can be executed by the existing pricing team within one quarter.
arguments_against: Does nothing about the underlying input-cost shock, so margin remains exposed if base oil continues to inflate faster than repricing cadence.
key_questions: Has the price-lock register been validated against every contract slated for repricing?

arguments_for: Renewal-cycle indexation is a durable structural change to contract architecture, not just a tactical price move.
arguments_against: If engine-oil category margins are in structural decline, repricing defends a position that may warrant a participation review instead.
key_questions: Are competitors passing through the same base-oil inflation, or is this a firm-specific cost disadvantage?

implementation_triggers: Price-lock contract register validated and repricing list cleared of all anchor accounts
Competitor pricing scan confirms market-wide pass-through of base-oil inflation
prerequisites: Legal review of every targeted contract against the mid-quarter price-lock clause before any escalation notice
Segmentation of Synthetic Blend revenue into spot vs contracted volume
Renewal calendar for anchor accounts with pass-through clause language drafted

impact_estimate.basis: A 3–4% ASP lift on spot Synthetic Blend volume plus renewal-cycle pass-through clauses recovers 2.5–4.2pp of the observed 7.14pp segment decline; partial because price-locked anchor volume (~40–50%) is unaddressable mid-quarter.

key_assumptions.assumption: Spot/transactional volume is large enough (~50%+ of Synthetic Blend revenue) for a 3–4% ASP lift to move segment margin materially.
key_assumptions.provenance: Revenue split of Synthetic Blend between spot and price-locked contracted volume, from order-level data.

key_assumptions.assumption: A 3–4% price increase will not trigger volume loss exceeding the margin gain.
key_assumptions.provenance: Post-repricing units_sold trend on repriced accounts vs held-out accounts over two periods.

key_assumptions.assumption: Price/mix movements pass through to Gross Margin % as the ratio's numerator.
key_assumptions.provenance: Confirmed client relationship: net_revenue <-> gross_margin_pct (direct, confirmed).

flagged_side_effects: Original proposal did not exclude price-locked anchor accounts from repricing; this option now hard-gates all repricing against the contract register, restricting escalation to spot customers and moving anchor-account changes to renewal windows only.

options_ranked.title: Anchor-Account Contract Restructuring — Volume Tiers and Mix Incentives with Rebate-Economics Guardrails
options_ranked.description: For anchor accounts locked out of mid-quarter repricing, restructure commercial terms via volume-tier and mix-shift incentives (e.g., rebates conditional on shifting volume toward higher-margin formulations), preceded by a base-oil pass-through audit that quantifies how much of the 7.14pp decline is recoverable via contract structure. Two guardrails are built in: (a) the mix-to-margin lift is treated as a hypothesis to validate with actual product-level margin data, not a fact, because the premium-mix relationship is an unconfirmed industry prior; (b) every rebate design must pass a net-economics test proving the rebate accrual (which reduces net revenue, a confirmed margin driver) is smaller than the margin gained from the mix or velocity change. Spot customers and within-threshold products are out of scope.
options_ranked.rationale: This is the only mechanism that reaches price-locked anchor volume without violating the constraint, because it changes economics via rebate structure rather than unit list price. Consistency check: the mix-shift target (premium formulations) is directionally supported — Engine Oils line margin (26.03%) still exceeds Value-category margin (19.82%) even after the decline — but the size of the mix-to-margin lift rests on an unconfirmed prior, so a per-account margin validation step precedes rollout.

arguments_for: Reaches the ~40–50% of volume that neither repricing nor short-term procurement action can protect, converting the price-lock constraint into a contract-design opportunity.
The pass-through audit doubles as the structural-vs-cyclical diagnostic needed for any future participation decision on the Value category.
arguments_against: Customer participation in rebate-for-mix programs is uncertain and may skew toward accounts that would have shifted mix anyway, paying rebates for behavior that was free.
key_questions: What is the current-state margin spread between premium formulations and Synthetic Blend at the account level, after the cost shock?

arguments_for: Restructured terms at anchor accounts create renewal-cycle leverage for embedding indexation clauses later.
arguments_against: Rebate accruals are booked as reductions to net revenue — a confirmed direct margin driver — so poorly-designed tiers could erode the very margin they aim to recover.
key_questions: What breakeven rebate rate leaves net margin positive under conservative mix-shift uptake?

arguments_for: The upfront pass-through audit produces the cost-decomposition evidence all three options need.
arguments_against: Rebate administration adds process and accrual-accounting complexity that raises cost-to-serve on the affected accounts.
key_questions: Can finance accrue and true-up tiered rebates accurately at the account level with current systems?

implementation_triggers: Account-level margin data confirms premium formulations retain a margin advantage over Synthetic Blend/Conventional after the cost shock
Net-economics model shows rebate cost below expected mix-driven margin gain at conservative uptake
prerequisites: Base-oil pass-through audit quantifying the recoverable share of the 7.14pp decline
Validation of the premium-mix-to-margin relationship with actual product-level margin data (it is currently an unconfirmed industry prior)
Rebate net-economics model signed off by finance before any customer proposal
Legal confirmation that rebate restructuring does not breach the price-lock or trigger most-favored-customer clauses

impact_estimate.basis: Rebate-driven 5–8% mix shift toward higher-margin formulations plus order-velocity gains within anchor accounts recovers 2.5–4.2pp of the 7.14pp Synthetic Blend decline, net of rebate accrual costs; sized to the anchor-account portion of the affected segment.

key_assumptions.assumption: Shifting anchor-account mix toward premium formulations lifts blended gross margin.
key_assumptions.provenance: The premium_mix_pct <-> gross_margin_pct relationship is an unconfirmed template prior; validated by account-level margin comparison of premium vs blend formulations in current-period data.

key_assumptions.assumption: Rebate accruals will be smaller than the margin gained from mix shift and velocity, leaving net margin positive.
key_assumptions.provenance: Net-economics model reconciled against actuals after one rebate cycle; falsified if net_revenue reduction from accruals exceeds margin gain (net_revenue -> gross_margin_pct is confirmed).

key_assumptions.assumption: Anchor accounts will participate in volume/mix incentive programs at meaningful uptake rates.
key_assumptions.provenance: Signed amendments with at least two of the top five anchor accounts within 120 days.

flagged_side_effects: The mix-shift-to-margin mechanism rests on an unconfirmed industry prior, not validated data; expected recovery could be materially overstated, so account-level margin validation gates the rollout.

Rebates are booked as reductions to net revenue — a confirmed direct margin driver — meaning the incentive itself can erode margin; a mandatory net-economics breakeven test precedes every customer proposal.

solutions.recommendation_rationale: The synchronized declines in Synthetic Blend (-7.14pp), Conventional (-6.61pp), and Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) point to a common input-cost shock, and the only fully confirmed causal path to that root cause is base_oil_cost summing into COGS, which directly moves Gross Margin %. The procurement and cost-to-serve intervention attacks that confirmed chain with the highest recovery range (3.0–5.5pp) while remaining completely untouched by the anchor-account price-lock constraint that limits both commercial alternatives. Its COGS decomposition also produces the evidence base the spot-repricing and contract-restructuring plays require, making it the correct first move that sequences rather than excludes the other two.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % has dropped by 7.14 points year_to_date (current level 20.64 on the driving segment; enterprise margin fell from 34.43% to 29.94%, a -4.49pp net decline vs prior year_to_date).
problem_reframe.complication: The compression is not uniform: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (-7.14pp), Conventional Engine Oil (-6.61pp), Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) and the Value category (-6.42pp) are all deteriorating simultaneously, while other timeframe buckets remain within threshold — a pattern consistent with a common upstream input-cost shock rather than product-specific demand shifts. A contractual price-lock clause blocks mid-quarter list-price recovery on Lubricants anchor accounts, constraining the fastest commercial lever.
problem_reframe.question: How do we recover 2.5–5.5 points of gross margin on the engine-oil portfolio within the price-lock constraint — via cost-side action, selective repricing on unconstrained volume, or contract-structure redesign?
key_assumptions: The synchronized decline across three base-oil-intensive product lines indicates input-cost inflation as the dominant driver (COGS -> Gross Margin % is a confirmed relationship; base_oil_cost -> COGS is a confirmed component).
The price-lock clause binds only anchor-account list prices mid-quarter; spot/transactional volume and contract-renewal terms remain addressable.
The premium-mix-to-margin relationship is an unconfirmed industry prior and must not be relied on as a primary recovery mechanism without validation.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Whether the base-oil cost shock is a cyclical spike (favoring hedging and holding the portfolio) or a structural cost reset (favoring contract restructuring and eventual Value-category participation review) is undetermined.
unresolved_tensions.requires: Head of Procurement to deliver a base-oil cost decomposition since 2026-006 with a cyclical-vs-structural assessment to the CFO by end of Week 3.

unresolved_tensions.tension: Spot repricing and rebate restructuring both touch customer economics on overlapping accounts; uncoordinated rollout could send contradictory pricing signals to the market.

proposed_option.title: Tiered Price Escalation on Synthetic Blend SKUs via Selective Contract Renegotiation and Spot-Market Repricing
proposed_option.description: Identify and renegotiate renewal-cycle contracts on Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (the highest-margin product under normal conditions) to recover 4–5pp of margin through a two-tier mechanism: (1) escalate list pricing on spot/transactional customers not bound by mid-quarter price locks, targeting a 3–4% ASP lift; (2) negotiate contract renewals with anchor accounts to embed a base-oil cost-pass-through clause, effective at next renewal window. This preserves contractual relationships while capturing upstream cost inflation.
proposed_option.mechanism: Gross Margin % = (Net Revenue − COGS) / Net Revenue. Holding COGS constant, a 3–4% ASP increase on Synthetic Blend (the product with the largest margin delta) will recover 40–60 basis points of the 714bp loss. For renewal contracts, embedding a cost-escalation mechanism directly reduces future COGS pressure. The mechanism targets the confirmed COGS ↔ Gross Margin % relationship and the confirmed net_revenue ↔ gross_margin_pct relationship simultaneously.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil carries the largest absolute delta (−7.14pp). A 3–4% ASP increase on this product (assuming it represents ~25–30% of lubricant revenue mix) yields 75–120bp recovery; contract renegotiation on renewals prevents future 2–3pp deterioration, netting 2.5–4.2pp recovery against the observed 7.14pp loss. Recovery is partial because mid-quarter price-lock constraints prevent immediate repricing on ~40–50% of anchor-account volume.

proposed_option.description: Initiate immediate supplier negotiations to lock in base oil pricing for the next contract renewal cycle, and evaluate forward hedging instruments (futures, swaps) to protect against further feedstock volatility. Simultaneously, conduct a cost-to-serve deep dive on Synthetic Blend and Conventional grades to identify non-material cost reduction levers (manufacturing yield, packaging optimization, distribution consolidation) that can be deployed within the price-lock window to recover 3–5 pp of margin without violating contractual constraints.

Since list prices cannot be raised mid-quarter, the intervention targets the numerator (COGS reduction via procurement hedging, supplier terms renegotiation, and internal process efficiency) rather than the denominator (revenue, which is contractually constrained). This preserves compliance with the price-lock clause while addressing the root cost shock.

impact_estimate.basis: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil declined 7.14 pp; recovery target of 3.0–5.5 pp reflects partial mitigation through supplier renegotiation (1.5–2.5 pp), forward hedging to stabilize future input costs (0.8–1.5 pp), and internal process optimization in manufacturing/packaging (0.7–1.5 pp). Full recovery to 27.78% is unlikely within 90 days due to price-lock constraint; recovery is phased across the repricing window.

proposed_option.title: Conduct Base Oil Cost & Supplier Pass-Through Analysis + Prepare Volume-Based Rebate Restructuring
proposed_option.description: Immediately audit base oil procurement costs (WTI-linked, supplier contract terms) and distribution/packaging line items to quantify the cost inflation magnitude. In parallel, model a volume-rebate restructuring for anchor accounts (those under price-lock) that shifts margin recovery from per-unit pricing to volume tiers or service bundling, preserving contract compliance while creating economic incentive to offset cost pressure through higher order velocity or mix shift toward higher-margin formulations.
proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil cost inflation is a direct COGS driver (confirmed relationship: base_oil_cost → COGS). The price-lock constraint prevents list-price recovery mid-quarter, but volume-based rebate restructuring (e.g., 'hit volume target, earn margin rebate' or 'shift 10% of volume to High Mileage, earn rebate') creates a workaround mechanism that maintains contractual compliance while recovering margin through mix or velocity without raising the unit price. This addresses the root cause (input cost) rather than symptoms (discounting or de-emphasis).

impact_estimate.basis: Base oil cost inflation likely accounts for 50–70% of the observed 7.14pp decline in Synthetic Blend. Volume-rebate restructuring targeting a 5–8% shift in mix toward higher-margin formulations or a 3–5% increase in order velocity within anchor accounts could recover 2.5–4.2pp of the margin loss, contingent on customer participation and execution speed within the 0–90 day window.
